desc: Project Magnet was approved by the Canadian Department of Transport on 2 December 1950 following Wilbert Smith's memorandum of 21 November 1950. Its stated goal was to collect data on UFOs and apply anything recovered to practical engineering - specifically to test whether the Earth's magnetic field could be exploited as a propulsion source, which Smith believed the objects were already doing. It drew on Department of Transport facilities with assistance from the Defence Research Board and the National Research Council; Smith's collaborators included Dr James Watt of the DRB, John Thompson of the DOT, Professor J. T. Wilson of the University of Toronto and Dr G. D. Garland of the Dominion Observatory. Its 1952 report is the document that matters: it concluded that the objects were about a hundred feet or more in diameter, capable of several thousand miles per hour and of altitudes above those supporting conventional aircraft or balloons, that 'we are forced to the conclusion that the vehicles are probably extra-terrestrial, in spite of our prejudices to the contrary', and that the next step should be 'a substantial effort towards the acquisition of as much as possible of this technology, which would without doubt be of great value to us'. That is a government engineer, in writing, in 1952, recommending a reverse-engineering programme. In October 1952 Smith set up an instrumented observatory at Shirley's Bay outside Ottawa with a magnetometer, gamma-ray detector, radio receiver, gravity meter and recorders. The Department terminated funding in 1954; Smith continued privately until his death in 1962.
